When Being a Teenager Starts to Feel Harder Than It Should

The teenage years can bring significant emotional, social and developmental changes.

School expectations, friendships, relationships, family changes, identity, social pressures and increasing independence can all contribute to stress. Feeling worried, overwhelmed, frustrated or low from time to time can be part of growing up.

But sometimes these feelings become more persistent or begin to interfere with everyday life.

Perhaps your teenager has stopped enjoying things they used to enjoy, is withdrawing from friends, constantly worrying about school or the future, struggling to sleep, feeling exhausted, becoming unusually irritable, or finding it increasingly difficult to cope.

You may be wondering:

Is this a difficult period of adolescence, or is my teenager experiencing anxiety or depression?

It is not always easy to tell.

Adolescents may not always describe what they are experiencing as anxiety or depression. Changes in behaviour, motivation, friendships, sleep, school participation or communication may be the first signs that something is not quite right.

Your teenager does not have to wait until things become overwhelming before seeking support.

Early support can help adolescents understand what they are experiencing, develop practical coping skills and find healthier ways to manage difficult emotions and situations.

Could This Be What Your Teenager Is Experiencing?

Anxiety and Depression Can Look Different in Every Teenager

Adolescents can experience anxiety, depression, or both at the same time.

Anxiety may involve persistent worry, fear, apprehension, physical tension, difficulty concentrating, reassurance-seeking or avoiding situations that feel overwhelming.

Depression can involve more than feeling sad. It may affect motivation, enjoyment, energy, concentration, sleep, relationships, school participation and the way a teenager views themselves or their future.

You may notice that your teenager:

  • seems persistently worried, tense or on edge
  • spends a lot of time overthinking or anticipating something going wrong
  • worries excessively about school, friendships, relationships, appearance, family or the future
  • avoids social situations or activities they previously enjoyed
  • becomes increasingly withdrawn from family or friends
  • seems unusually irritable, frustrated or emotionally overwhelmed
  • has lost interest in activities they once enjoyed
  • appears persistently sad, flat, empty or low
  • has noticeably less motivation or energy
  • struggles to concentrate or make decisions
  • experiences changes in sleep
  • experiences changes in appetite or eating patterns
  • complains of headaches, stomach aches, nausea or other physical symptoms
  • experiences changes in school attendance, participation or performance
  • frequently describes feeling overwhelmed, hopeless or unable to cope
  • seems very self-critical or feels that they are not good enough
  • finds everyday responsibilities increasingly difficult to manage

Not every teenager experiencing anxiety or depression will show the same signs.

Some adolescents may continue performing well at school or appearing socially confident while struggling internally.

You May Be Looking for Support Because...

You may be here because something about your teenager has changed.

Perhaps:

  • they no longer seem like themselves
  • school has become increasingly difficult
  • they are avoiding friends, activities or situations they once enjoyed
  • they are constantly worried about what other people think
  • they seem overwhelmed by school or everyday expectations
  • they are struggling with friendships or relationships
  • they are spending more time alone
  • their motivation has noticeably decreased
  • sleep has become difficult or significantly changed
  • they seem persistently irritable, sad or emotionally exhausted
  • they are finding it difficult to concentrate
  • they are frequently saying that they cannot cope
  • conversations at home have become increasingly difficult
  • you are unsure whether what you are seeing is typical teenage behaviour or something more significant
  • your teenager has said they would like someone outside the family to talk to

You do not need to diagnose your teenager before seeking support.

A qualified professional can help you understand what may be happening and whether anxiety, depression, another mental health concern, or a combination of factors may be contributing.

Understanding Adolescent Anxiety & Depression

Why Can Mental Health Become More Difficult During Adolescence?

There is rarely one single cause of anxiety or depression.

Adolescent mental health is influenced by a combination of biological, psychological, social and environmental factors.

Adolescence itself is an important developmental period involving rapid emotional, social and cognitive changes. At the same time, teenagers are developing greater independence and navigating new responsibilities, relationships and expectations.

Depending on the individual, contributing factors may include:

Developmental Changes

Adolescence involves significant changes in emotions, thinking, relationships and independence. These changes can create new challenges while teenagers are still developing ways to manage stress and difficult emotions.

School and Academic Pressure

Schoolwork, examinations, performance expectations, attendance and uncertainty about the future can contribute to stress and anxiety.

Friendships and Relationships

Friendship difficulties, conflict, rejection, loneliness or changes in relationships can have a significant emotional impact during adolescence.

Social Expectations

Teenagers may feel pressure to fit in, meet expectations, compare themselves with others or present themselves in particular ways.

Family and Life Changes

Family conflict, separation, changes at home, financial difficulties, relocation, illness or other significant life events can affect adolescent wellbeing.

Bullying and Social Isolation

Negative experiences with peers, bullying, exclusion or feeling disconnected from others can contribute to psychological distress.

Trauma or Difficult Experiences

Experiences of trauma, loss, abuse or other significant adversity can affect mental health and may contribute to anxiety or depression.

Physical and Mental Health Factors

Sleep difficulties, chronic health conditions and co-occurring mental health concerns can also affect emotional wellbeing.

Social Media and the Digital Environment

The digital environment can introduce additional social pressures. The Australian Counselling Association's 2026 discussion of Australia's Health 2026 highlighted concerns around excessive social media use, including possible contributions to isolation, inadequacy and dissatisfaction. These factors do not mean that a teenager will necessarily develop anxiety or depression. They are part of a much broader picture that needs to be considered individually.

When Anxiety and Low Mood Start to Affect Everyday Life

The Impact Can Extend Beyond How Someone Feels

Anxiety and depression can affect more than mood.

They can influence the way a teenager thinks, behaves, relates to other people and manages everyday responsibilities.

School and Learning

A teenager may find it harder to concentrate, make decisions, complete work, attend school or maintain their usual level of participation.

Friendships and Relationships

They may withdraw from friends, avoid social situations, become more sensitive to rejection or find communication more difficult.

Family Life

Irritability, withdrawal, changes in communication or reduced participation at home can affect family relationships.

Sleep and Energy

Anxiety and depression can affect sleep, energy and motivation, making everyday tasks feel more difficult.

Confidence and Self-Perception

Persistent worry or low mood can influence how teenagers view themselves, their abilities and their future.

Enjoyment and Motivation

Depression can reduce interest in activities that previously provided enjoyment or connection.

Overall Functioning

When symptoms persist, they can begin affecting education, relationships, physical wellbeing and participation in everyday life.

Australian data show that mental health conditions among young people can have significant effects on education, employment, relationships and daily functioning, reinforcing the importance of early identification and appropriate support.

You Don't Have to Figure It Out Alone

Supporting Your Teenager Through a Difficult Period

It can be difficult for parents to know when to step in.

Teenagers are developing independence and may want greater privacy around their thoughts and emotions. At the same time, they may need support to recognise when something is becoming difficult to manage alone.

Professional therapy can provide a space where a teenager can talk openly with someone outside their immediate family.

Depending on their individual needs, therapy may help an adolescent:

  • understand anxiety, low mood and emotional responses
  • identify patterns of thinking that may be contributing to distress
  • develop practical coping strategies
  • improve emotional regulation
  • manage stress and uncertainty
  • build problem-solving skills
  • improve communication
  • strengthen confidence and self-understanding
  • gradually approach situations they have been avoiding
  • develop healthier routines and coping strategies
  • reconnect with activities, relationships and goals that are meaningful to them

The goal is not to eliminate every difficult emotion.

It is to help a teenager develop the understanding, skills and support they need to manage difficult experiences and continue moving forward.

What Could Change with the Right Support?

Helping Your Teenager Feel More Capable

Therapy does not mean that something is "wrong" with your teenager.

It can provide an opportunity to understand what is happening and develop strategies that make everyday life more manageable.

With appropriate support, a teenager may become better able to:

  • recognise early signs of anxiety or low mood
  • understand the connection between thoughts, emotions and behaviour
  • communicate what they are experiencing
  • manage difficult emotions
  • cope with uncertainty and everyday stress
  • challenge unhelpful thinking patterns
  • approach situations they have been avoiding
  • improve problem-solving skills
  • strengthen relationships
  • rebuild motivation and engagement
  • develop greater confidence in managing challenges

The goal is not to create a life without stress or difficult emotions. It is to help your teenager feel more capable of navigating them.

For Parents

Supporting Your Teenager While Respecting Their Independence

Supporting an adolescent can feel different from supporting a younger child.

Teenagers are developing independence, forming their own opinions and learning to manage more of their lives themselves.

Parents still have an important role, but support may involve listening, staying connected and helping a teenager access appropriate professional care rather than trying to solve everything for them.

Depending on the situation, parents may benefit from learning how to:

  • listen without immediately trying to solve the problem
  • take concerns seriously without increasing fear
  • encourage appropriate professional support
  • maintain open communication
  • support healthy routines around sleep, activity and daily life
  • recognise changes in behaviour and functioning
  • encourage connection with trusted people
  • respect growing independence while maintaining appropriate support
  • work with the treating professional where appropriate and with the teenager's consent

You do not need to have the perfect response.

Sometimes the most important step is helping your teenager know that they do not have to manage everything alone.

What Could Treatment Look Like?

Individualised Therapy for Anxiety and Depression

There is no single treatment that is appropriate for every teenager.

Treatment should be guided by the adolescent's symptoms, circumstances, developmental stage, goals and level of impairment.

A mental health assessment can help determine the most appropriate approach.

Psychological Therapy

Psychological therapy is an important treatment option for adolescent anxiety and depression.

Depending on the presentation, therapy may include approaches such as cognitive behavioural therapy (CBT), counselling, behavioural strategies, acceptance-based approaches or other evidence-based psychological interventions.

CBT can help adolescents understand connections between thoughts, feelings and behaviours and develop more helpful ways of responding. It is well established as a psychological treatment for anxiety, and psychological treatment is generally preferred before medication for adolescent anxiety.

Developing Coping and Emotional Regulation Skills

Therapy may focus on recognising emotions, managing stress, improving problem-solving and developing practical strategies that can be used outside the therapy room.

Gradual Behavioural Change

Where anxiety is contributing to avoidance, therapy may involve gradual and planned steps towards situations the teenager has been avoiding.

The aim is not to force a teenager into situations they find overwhelming.

It is to develop confidence and coping skills at a manageable pace.

Family Involvement

Depending on the teenager's age, circumstances and treatment approach, parents or caregivers may be involved in aspects of therapy.

This can help families understand what is happening and create a supportive environment outside appointments.

Medication

Medication is not automatically required for adolescent anxiety or depression.

For anxiety disorders, Australian Prescriber identifies psychological therapy as the treatment of first choice, with antidepressants generally considered when psychological therapy has not been effective or cannot be engaged with.

For moderate to severe depression, medication may sometimes form part of treatment following professional assessment. Decisions about antidepressants in adolescents require careful consideration and monitoring by an appropriately qualified medical professional.

Medication decisions should always be made with the treating doctor or psychiatrist.

When Should You Seek Professional Support?

You Don't Have to Wait Until Things Become Severe

It may be appropriate to seek professional support when anxiety or low mood:

  • persists for several weeks or longer
  • is becoming more frequent or intense
  • affects school attendance or participation
  • affects friendships or relationships
  • interferes with sleep
  • significantly changes motivation or energy
  • reduces enjoyment of previously valued activities
  • leads to increasing avoidance or withdrawal
  • affects concentration or everyday functioning
  • creates significant distress for the teenager or family
  • is becoming difficult for the teenager to manage independently

Raising Children Network notes that depression in adolescents is more than ordinary sadness or moodiness, and that the duration, intensity and impact on school, relationships, physical health and everyday activities are important considerations.

If you are unsure, you can still reach out.

You do not need to know whether your teenager has anxiety, depression or another condition before asking for professional guidance.

When Anxiety and Depression Occur Together

Sometimes It's More Complicated Than One Concern

Anxiety and depression can occur together.

A teenager may experience persistent worry while also losing motivation, withdrawing from friends or feeling increasingly low.

The Australian Counselling Association reported in 2026 that around 30% of adolescents with a mental illness experienced two or more mental health concerns within the same 12-month period.

This is one reason an individual assessment can be valuable.

Rather than focusing only on one symptom, a qualified practitioner can consider the broader picture, including:

  • what the teenager has been experiencing
  • when the changes began
  • what may be contributing to them
  • how symptoms are affecting everyday functioning
  • existing strengths and supports
  • whether other concerns may also be present
  • what type of treatment or support may be appropriate

Adolescent Mental Health in Australia

Why Early Support Matters in 2026

Mental health concerns during adolescence are an important public health issue in Australia.

The Australian Institute of Health and Welfare reports that almost 39% of young people aged 16-24 experienced a mental disorder in the previous 12 months in 2020-2022, up from 26% in 2007. Anxiety disorders were the most common mental health conditions among young people.

The 2026 Australia's Health report also identifies a significant rise in mental disorders among young people and highlights the continuing need for prevention, early identification and access to appropriate care.

Burnet Institute modelling published in 2026 projected that, without stronger prevention efforts, one in two Australian teenagers could experience anxiety or depression by age 20. The modelling also found that investment in prevention could substantially reduce the number of young Australians experiencing these conditions.

These figures do not mean that every teenager will develop a mental health condition.

They highlight why recognising changes early, talking openly about mental health and making appropriate support accessible can matter.

You Don't Need to Know Where to Start

Finding the Right Support for Your Teenager

It can be difficult to know whether your teenager needs psychological therapy, an assessment, family support, a GP review or another form of care.

You don't need to diagnose your teenager before contacting us.

You can tell us what you have noticed, what your teenager has been experiencing and how these concerns are affecting everyday life.

Our team can help gather the relevant information and guide you towards an appropriate practitioner or support pathway based on your teenager's needs.

Whether your teenager is experiencing persistent anxiety, low mood, social withdrawal, school-related stress, loss of motivation, relationship difficulties, significant worry, or a combination of concerns, we can help you explore the next step.

Why Families Choose MBP

Clinically Informed Support, With Adolescents and Families at the Centre

Michelle Barratt Psychology & Administrative Services (MBP) provides a professional and supportive entry point for families seeking psychological and allied health care.

Our role is to make accessing support clearer and more manageable while helping families connect with practitioners whose experience aligns with their teenager's needs.

Clinically Informed Intake

Our intake process helps us understand the concerns you are seeking support for and identify an appropriate pathway.

Adolescent-Focused Matching

We help families identify practitioners who work with adolescents and whose experience is relevant to the concerns described.

Family Support

We assist parents and caregivers with referrals, appointments, intake requirements and administrative processes.

Respect for Adolescent Development

Adolescents are not simply younger children. Their growing independence, relationships, communication style and developmental stage are important considerations when identifying appropriate support.

Coordinated Support

Where appropriate and with the necessary consent, practitioners may liaise with GPs, schools and other professionals involved in your teenager's care.

Flexible Access

In-person appointments are available across Brisbane, with telehealth options available Australia-wide where clinically appropriate and offered by the practitioner.

Your Teenager Doesn't Have to Work Through It Alone

Maybe you have noticed that your teenager has become more withdrawn.

Maybe school has become harder, friendships have changed, sleep has become difficult, or they no longer seem interested in things they used to enjoy.

Or perhaps they have told you that they are constantly worried, overwhelmed or struggling to cope.

You don't need to have all the answers before reaching out.

Start by telling us a little about what you have been noticing and what you would like support with.

We'll help you understand the next steps and explore an appropriate pathway for your teenager. Contact Michelle Barratt Psychology to learn more about adolescent anxiety and depression support.
